name: Bankura Terracotta
tagline: Clay horses from Panchmura and clay-brick temples from Bishnupur, shaped by potters.
facts: Bankura horse: long-necked terracotta horse from Panchmura
GI registered 28 March 2018 as Bankura Panchmura Terracotta Craft
Makers: potters of the Kumbhakar (kumhar) community
Bishnupur's terracotta temples date from the Malla kings, about 17th-18th century
art: Bankura is known for two kinds of terracotta, a word that means baked earth. One is the Bankura horse: a stylised horse with a long neck, a small head and pointed ears, made in Panchmura village. The other is the carved terracotta panels on the temples of Bishnupur.

The Bankura horse is made by hand. Sources describe a hollow body built in parts and fired, with the larger horses in two or more pieces. The horse is often offered to village gods in the region as a votive gift, and it has also become a symbol of Bengal craft sold around India. Potters also make elephants and other figures.
The horse was registered as a Geographical Indication on 28 March 2018 under the name Bankura Panchmura Terracotta Craft, according to published sources.

At Bishnupur the temples are built of laterite and brick, and clay plaques fixed on the walls show scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and the Krishna stories, as well as scenes from daily life. The Rasmancha is among the earliest surviving of them. Sources differ on the number of temples: one scholarly count cited in a source says there were once as many as 450 terracotta and laterite temples in Bishnupur, and about 20 survive today.
artist: The Bankura horse is made by potters of the Kumbhakar community. Sources credit the potters of Panchmura with the development of the distinctive long-necked horse.

The work is often a family affair, with men shaping and firing and women and children helping with clay preparation and finishing. I did not find a reliable count of the families in Panchmura, and sources give different figures.
Some potters have worked with craft councils and government bodies to reach buyers. Specific names and awards should be added only after checking with the artists directly.
Bishnupur's temple plaques were made by local craftsmen under the Malla kings. I did not find the names of those artisans in the sources.
place: Bankura is in the western part of West Bengal, where the plain of Bengal gives way to the laterite plateau. The red soil is poor for farming but it supplies clay and building stone.
Panchmura is a village in Bankura district, reported as roughly 20 km from Bishnupur, though sources give different distances. Potters here make horses and also tiles and domestic pots.

Bishnupur was the capital of the Malla kings, who patronised terracotta and built temples to Krishna and Vishnu, mostly in the 17th and 18th centuries. Reports differ on whether the temples have been nominated to UNESCO, and I could not verify the current status.

history.what: Terracotta horse offerings are old in Bengal. One source claims a start in the 7th century, but that claim is weakly sourced.
The Malla kings of Bishnupur begin building brick and terracotta temples. The Rasmancha is dated by some sources to about 1600.
Most of the Bishnupur temple plaques are made. The kingdom later declines.
Panchmura's horses become known as a craft symbol of Bengal and are promoted by craft bodies.
Bankura Panchmura Terracotta Craft is registered as a GI.
Potters sell horses and other items at fairs, shops and online; the Bishnupur temples are visited by tourists.

future: Create a potters' cooperative with direct sales and fair prices.
Train young potters in design, firing and business, while keeping the traditional forms alive.
Use the GI mark to separate hand-made Panchmura work from mass-produced copies.
Fund repair of Bishnupur's temples by the ASI and local bodies, with skilled terracotta restorers hired locally.
Offer village visits where visitors see clay digging, shaping and firing, with income going to the families.
Study and record the number of working potters and the state of the temples, so that policy is based on facts.

name: Bishnupur Terracotta Temples
tagline: Burnt-brick temples of the Malla kings, covered in clay panels of Krishna, epics and daily life.
facts: Built by Malla kings, mainly 17th and 18th centuries
On UNESCO's tentative list since 1997
Bricks and terracotta plaques used because stone was scarce
Last Malla temple: Radheshyam, 1758
art: Bishnupur's temples are built of brick and laterite and decorated with terracotta plaques. Sahapedia explains that stone was scarce, so builders made bricks of different shapes for different parts of a building. The clay came from the Ganga delta.

The plaques show Krishna's life, especially the rasachakra dance and the nine gopis who form an elephant. They also show the Ramayana, Mahabharata, Puranas and the ten avatars of Vishnu. Everyday scenes appear too, with musicians, dancers, soldiers, animals, clothing and jewellery.
The Shyamrai temple, built by Raghunath Singha, is a pancharatna temple with about 5,000 tiles, the most elaborate in the town. Jorbangla (1655) and Kalachand (1656) are also his.
artist: The sculptors are unnamed. Sahapedia says artisans worked in groups led by supervisors, with sculptors, designers and writers each having a role.

The patrons are named. Bir Hambir began the Vaishnava temples after turning to Gaudiya Vaishnavism. Raghunath Singha, Bir Singha II and Durjan Singh built more, and queens such as Chudamanidevi and Shiromanidevi paid for others.
Today the craft continues in smaller form: Wikipedia says Bishnupur is known for terracotta horses and figurines.
place: Bishnupur is a town in Bankura district, West Bengal, once the capital of Mallabhum. Wikipedia says it was placed on UNESCO's tentative list in 1997.

The town is also known for Baluchari saris, whose pallav scenes were influenced by the temples, and for the Bishnupur gharana of dhrupad music. Some temples remain places of worship; Malleshwar now houses Shiva.

history.what: Sahapedia says the Mallas ruled Mallabhum for centuries and that Bir Hambir began the Vaishnava temple building.
Malleshwar temple, a laterite deul, built by Bir Hambir.
Raghunath Singha's Jorbangla (1655) and Kalachand (1656), and Bir Singha II's Lalji (1658).
Madangopal and Muralimohan, paid for by queens.
Madanmohan, built by Durjan Singh, noted for terracotta tiles.
Radheshyam, the last Malla temple.
The dynasty declined, hit by weak rulers, money shortages and rising zamindars.

future: Training: teach terracotta carving and conservation to local youth.
Livelihood: guided visits and craft sales that return income to town artisans.
Materials: use compatible clay and lime for repairs.
Documentation: map every panel; Sahapedia notes many have lost ornament, for example at Madangopal.
Protection: ASI care continues; the UNESCO tentative listing awaits a full nomination.

name: Chola Bronzes
tagline: Gods cast in metal from a wax model, as they were in Chola temples a thousand years ago.
facts: Technique: lost-wax casting (madhuchchishta vidhana)
Metal: panchaloha, an alloy of five metals
Famous image: Shiva as Nataraja, Lord of the Dance
Swamimalai bronze icons carry a GI tag (about 2008-09)
art: Chola bronzes are metal images of gods and goddesses made in the Kaveri river delta of Tamil Nadu. The Cholas ruled much of south India from about the 9th to the 13th century, and the finest early images are linked to their temples. Many were made as processional images (utsava murti), carried out of the temple on festival days.

The method is lost-wax casting, called madhuchchishta vidhana in the Sanskrit craft texts. The maker models the figure in a mix of beeswax and resin, coats it in layers of fine river clay to make a mould, and heats it so the wax melts out. Molten metal is then poured into the empty space. The mould is broken to free the image, and the maker chases, files and polishes it. Each cast is therefore a single piece: the mould cannot be reused.

The metal is panchaloha, usually described as an alloy of five metals. Sources differ on exactly which five and in what mix, and craft workshops describe mainly copper with tin and other metals, sometimes with small amounts of silver or gold. Treat any one recipe as a workshop tradition, not a fixed rule.

The best known image is the Nataraja, Shiva dancing within a ring of flames, one foot raised, the other on a small figure of forgetfulness. Other subjects include Parvati, Vishnu with Sri and Bhu, Ganesha, Kali, and Shaiva saints such as the Nayanmars. Images follow proportions set down in the Shilpa Shastra texts.

Sources describe the Chola figures as slender and graceful, with soft modelling of the body and fine jewellery. Today the same technique is used by workshops in Swamimalai, whose bronze icons were registered under the Geographical Indications scheme; sources give about 2008-09, but disagree on the application number, so check the GI Registry before quoting it.
artist: The traditional makers are called sthapathis. Sources describe them as belonging to the Vishwakarma community of hereditary craftspeople, with skills passed down within families over many generations. Swamimalai, near Kumbakonam, is the best known centre.

The work is a team effort. One person may model the wax, another prepare the clay and the furnace, and others finish the cast. The sthapathi is also responsible for getting the proportions and iconography right, and for the ritual side of making a god-image.

Local lore connects the craft with the building of the great Thanjavur temple, when sthapathis are said to have been trained in the lost-wax method. This is tradition, not documented history, and I could not verify it from a primary source.

Workshops today make images for temples and for buyers across India and abroad. Some training now also happens in government institutions of traditional art. I did not find reliable figures on how many families still practise, which needs local research.
place: The Kaveri delta in Tamil Nadu is among the most fertile parts of south India. The river brought the clay for moulds and the wealth that paid for temples. Thanjavur, Kumbakonam and nearby towns were the heart of the Chola country.

Swamimalai is a small town a few kilometres from Kumbakonam, known for its hilltop Murugan temple and its workshops. The river clay used for moulds is often said to be taken from the Kaveri banks, a detail workshops stress as part of their identity.

Chola kings and queens gave temples land, money and metal images. The Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur and the temples of Kumbakonam, Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram are linked with the same age. The demand for processional bronzes grew with the festival life of these temples, which is why the art grew here.

history.what: Small metal images were made in south India under the Pallavas. Scholars link them to the later Chola style but dates of individual pieces are debated.
The Cholas rise in the Kaveri delta and begin building stone temples that need processional images.
Queen Sembiyan Mahadevi is often credited with patronising temple building and bronze images. Details come mostly from temple inscriptions and later scholarship.
Rajaraja I and Rajendra I build great temples at Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram. Many bronzes in museums are dated to the 10th to 12th centuries.
Chola power declines. Bronze casting continues in temple workshops.
Chola bronzes become widely known as museum pieces in India and abroad. Some temple images have been stolen and later returned or traced, a continuing concern.
Swamimalai bronze icons are registered as a Geographical Indication.
Swamimalai workshops continue hereditary casting; the craft depends on temple orders and the art market.

future: Support apprenticeships so young people can learn modelling, casting and finishing within families and workshops, with a recognised certificate.
Help sthapathis reach buyers directly, with fair pricing and clear GI marks so that machine or imitation castings are not sold as hand work.
Record the ritual and technical knowledge, including the material mix, in plain language with the makers' consent.
Protect temple bronzes with photographic records, secure storage and community-run trusts, to prevent theft.
Open workshops to visitors with guided demonstrations, so people see a cast broken from its mould.
Keep clay and metal supply sustainable: fair rates for scrap metal, and safe furnaces for workers.

name: Dhokra
tagline: Lost-wax metal casting, thousands of years in the making.
facts: Medium: brass and bell metal
Method: lost-wax casting, one mould one piece
Subject: animals, deities, tribal life
art: Dhokra (also spelt Dokra) figures are made by hand-shaping a clay core, covering it with wax threads, wrapping it in clay, heating it so that the wax melts away and then pouring molten metal into the cavity. The mould must be broken to reveal the work, so no two pieces are the same.
The coiled wax-thread surface gives the metal its characteristic texture.
artist: The craft is practised by communities such as the Ghadwa of Bastar, and the Dhokra Damar tribes of West Bengal and Odisha, whose name gave the craft its name.
The skill is passed from parent to child; the whole family works, from preparing clay to polishing.
Our approach: show the kiln, the wax and the family as part of each story.
place: Bastar in southern Chhattisgarh is a forested adivasi region; related centres are in Odisha, West Bengal (Dariapur) and Jharkhand.
The Dhokra Damars were historically a nomadic community, which spread the technique across eastern India.

history.what: The bronze 'Dancing Girl' of Mohenjo-daro is often cited as an early example of lost-wax casting in the subcontinent.
The technique continued through tribal metalworkers.
Handicraft boards and fairs sell Dhokra widely; cheap imitations are a challenge.

future: Secure metal supply: community-owned buying to reduce raw material costs.
Document the Dhokra Damar migration routes as a living map.
Differentiate genuine pieces with maker tags.

name: Diu Stone Carving
states: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
tagline: Sandstone fort walls and Baroque churches on a small island off the Kathiawar coast.
facts: Place: Diu island, off Gujarat
Diu Fort: begun 1535 by the Portuguese, in sandstone and lime mortar
St Paul's Church: completed 1610
I found no documented craft of living stone carvers in Diu
art: This is a short entry because I could not find a study or official page that describes a stone-carving craft in Diu as a living tradition. What is documented is the built stone of the island.

Wikipedia says the Diu Fort was built in sandstone and lime mortar. It skirts the sea on three sides and has a double moat, three gates and bastions with gun mounts. The same page notes only a Portuguese inscription at the entrance gate and does not describe decorative carving.
Diu is also known for Portuguese Baroque churches, including St Paul's Church, which is completed in 1610 and still in use according to Wikipedia.
Gujarat as a whole has a famous stone-carving tradition among Sompura temple builders, but I found no source that links it to Diu.
artist: I found no named stone carvers or families of Diu in any source I could read. The Incredible India page on Diu's arts and crafts did not load when I tried it.

Wikipedia says the fort was built with Portuguese forced labour, from October to March. It does not name the workers, and the story of the people who cut and laid this stone is not told in the sources I read.
place: Diu is a small island at the southern tip of the Kathiawar peninsula in Gujarat, joined to the mainland by a bridge. It is a fishing town, and the fort stands at its eastern end.
Portugal held Diu from 1535 until Indian forces took it in 1961. Diu has been part of the union territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu since the merger of 2020.

history.what: After the Treaty of Bassein, the Sultan of Gujarat agreed to let the Portuguese build a fort at Diu, to gain help against the Mughal ruler Humayun.
An Ottoman force besieged the fort and lifted the siege. Accounts differ on why.
The fort was strengthened and held against a second siege, under Dom Joao de Castro.
St Paul's Church was built in the Portuguese Baroque style.
Indian forces took Diu from Portugal.
Diu was merged with Dadra and Nagar Haveli in one union territory.

future: Survey the stone buildings of Diu, with measured drawings and photographs, and publish the results.
Find out whether any local families still cut or carve stone, and record their work before writing about it as a craft.
Train local youth in conservation masonry, using lime mortar and sandstone repairs on the fort and churches.
Keep the fort and churches in the care of heritage staff, with clear rules for visitors.
Give visitors a short, honest account of who built the fort and under what conditions.

name: French Colonial Architecture of Puducherry
tagline: A grid town where French villas and Tamil row houses stand on either side of a canal.
facts: French rule: 1674 to 1954, with brief Dutch and British periods
Dutch grid plan drawn 1693-1699; French finished it from 1700
French Quarter (Ville Blanche) and Tamil Quarter (Ville Noire)
INTACH and EFEO listed heritage buildings from 1987 to 1995
art: The old town of Puducherry is laid out as a grid inside four boulevards. A canal runs through it. Sahapedia explains that it began as a drainage channel and was also used by the French to separate communities by race and class.

East of the canal, the French Quarter has wide, tree-lined streets, large compounds and villas. Houses have pilasters, cornices, arched openings with louvred wooden shutters, wooden balconies on iron brackets and parapets. The pitched European roof gave way to the flat Madras terrace roof, which suits the climate. Most have a colonnaded portico, a walled garden or court, and high ceilings.

West of the canal, the Tamil Quarter has a denser street plan with back-to-back row houses. Its signature features are the thalvaram, a street veranda on wooden posts, and the thinnai, a masonry bench for visitors. The entry is by a carved doorway to a colonnaded courtyard called the mutram. Older houses are single-storey with country-tiled roofs, and later houses are two-storey with colonial touches.

INTACH says the two styles influenced each other and merged into a Franco-Tamil synthesis. The craft behind it is carved wood, iron work, plaster and masonry, though I did not find a source that names the builders or the materials used in the walls.
artist: The buildings were made by local masons, carpenters and ironworkers working to French and Tamil patterns. None of the sources I read names them, and I have not invented names.

Today the people who care for the buildings are owners, conservation architects and INTACH Pondicherry, which records heritage buildings through measured drawings and photographs. Its staff and the French research institute EFEO prepared the heritage list.
place: Puducherry lies on the Coromandel Coast of the Bay of Bengal. Its streets run in straight lines, east to west and north to south, with the sea on the east. French and Tamil names sit side by side on its street signs.

The French Quarter is by the sea and around Bharathi Park. The Tamil Quarter grew around temples in the north. A Muslim quarter in the south-west has streets angled so that mosques face Mecca, per Sahapedia.

history.what: French administration began, according to Sahapedia, and lasted until 1954 with brief Dutch and British control.
The Dutch drew up a grid plan for the town.
The French regained the town and completed it as a Boulevard Town.
French rule ended in practice, as the territory joined India.
INTACH and EFEO compiled a list of buildings of heritage value in the old town.
The list was revised to the Ministry of Environment and Forests' categories: I, II-A, II-B and III.

future: Support owners of heritage houses with grants, advice and skilled masons, especially in the Tamil Quarter where traditional houses are most at risk.
Train carpenters, ironworkers and plasterers in repair of period buildings.
Enforce heritage rules on new building and demolition within the boulevards.
Keep records of buildings through measured drawings and photographs, as INTACH does.
Tell the story of the Tamil and Franco-Tamil houses alongside the French villas, and the story of the canal's use to separate communities.

name: Hampi Sculpture
tagline: Granite gods, a stone chariot and a 6.7-metre Narasimha, left by the Vijayanagara capital.
facts: UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed 1986
Capital of Vijayanagara, 1336 to 1565
Granite and sandstone, carved on site
Famous works: stone chariot, Hazara Rama friezes, Narasimha monolith
art: Hampi's sculpture is carved in the local granite and sandstone, and much of it is part of the temple buildings. Wikipedia describes friezes, pillars, platforms and large figures cut on the spot from rock.

The stone chariot in the Vittala temple is a shrine to Garuda and the most pictured symbol of Hampi. Wikipedia notes that the temple's sabha mandapa has 56 carved beams that sound musical notes when struck. One travel source says the chariot is not exactly as it first looked; I did not find a scholarly source on that.

The Hazara Rama temple has friezes of the Ramayana. Its outer walls also show scenes of Mahanavami (Dasara) and Holi festivals. On the Mahanavami platform, the reliefs show marching elephants, horses, camels, musicians and dancers.

Some figures are monoliths. The Lakshmi Narasimha, a seated Yoga-Narasimha 6.7 metres tall, is carved in place near the Krishna temple. Two Ganesha figures on Hemakuta hill, the Kadalekalu (over 4.5 metres) and the Sasivekalu (2.4 metres), are also carved in place.
artist: The sculptors of Hampi are not named in the sources I read. Their work is known through the stone itself, and the names and workshops behind it are not recorded here.
The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) maintains the monuments and carries out excavations, per Wikipedia. I did not find a sourced account of present-day Hampi carvers and so leave that out.
place: Hampi lies on the Tungabhadra River in Vijayanagara district, in east-central Karnataka. The ground is rocky, with boulders and hills, and the granite shaped the carving. The site covers about 4,187 hectares with a larger buffer zone, and Wikipedia says about 1,600 surviving remains.
Wikipedia names the Vittala temple, the Hazara Rama temple, the Mahanavami platform and the Lotus Mahal, a two-storey pavilion that mixes Hindu and Indo-Islamic styles, among the key monuments.
The nearby village of Kinhal keeps a wood-painting tradition that its makers link with Hampi.

history.what: Hampi is capital of the Vijayanagara Empire.
After the Battle of Talikota, the capital is conquered and sacked, then left as ruins (Wikipedia).
UNESCO inscribes the Group of Monuments at Hampi under criteria (i), (iii) and (iv), reference 241.
The site is on the List of World Heritage in Danger (Wikipedia).
The ASI maintains the site and continues excavation.

future: Training: teach stone conservation and carving to local young people alongside ASI work.
Livelihood: make sure the visitors Hampi receives support local guides, craftspeople and families.
Materials: use matching local granite for repairs, following conservation guidance.
Documentation: keep photographing and cataloguing reliefs, and record what has changed since restoration.
Protection: manage the buffer zone so new building does not harm the monuments.

name: Harappan Art
tagline: Stone seals, tiny bronzes and clay animals from the Indus cities, with a script still unread.
facts: Period: mature phase about 2600 to 1900 BCE
Main forms: steatite seals, terracotta, bronze, beads
Sites in India: Dholavira, Lothal (Gujarat), Rakhigarhi (Haryana)
Dholavira: UNESCO World Heritage Site, 2021
art: The Indus or Harappan civilisation lasted from about 3300 to 1300 BCE, with its mature phase from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. Its art is small in scale and was made for daily and trade use.

Steatite seals show animals, human figures and signs of the Indus script, which is still undeciphered. They were used to stamp clay on trade goods. Terracotta includes figures of zebu, carts and chickens. Faience beads were made with materials from far away.

The Dancing Girl is a bronze, about 10.5 cm tall, made by lost-wax casting. It was found at Mohenjo-daro in 1926 and is in the National Museum in New Delhi. Jonathan Kenoyer argues that the dancer reading reflects a British colonial view and that she may be carrying an offering. The museum still calls her a dancer.

The Pashupati seal, found at Mohenjo-daro in 1928 or 1929, shows a seated figure with a horned headdress among animals. John Marshall read it as a proto-Shiva. Others have read it as a goddess or a buffalo-man. Wikipedia says many scholars think its meaning cannot be known.
artist: No makers are named. The craft workers of the Indus cities are known only through what they made. The Indus script cannot be read, so we have no names or voices.

Archaeologists give us the story of discovery. At Dholavira, a local man, Shambhudan Gadhvi, drew attention to the site in the early 1960s. J. P. Joshi of the ASI is credited with the official discovery in 1967 or 1968, and Ravindra Singh Bisht directed excavations from about 1989 to 1990.
At Dholavira, ten large gypsum signs were found that once stood on a wooden board about 3 m long. It is among the longest Indus inscriptions known.
place: The civilisation spread across much of Pakistan, north-western India and north-eastern Afghanistan. In India, Dholavira on Khadir Bet island in the Rann of Kutch, Lothal on the Gujarat coast and Rakhigarhi in Haryana are major sites. Dholavira and Rakhigarhi are two of five major urban centres.

Dholavira was a walled city of about 47 hectares. It had sixteen or more stone-cut reservoirs and a drainage system. UNESCO inscribed it in 2021 as Dholavira: A Harappan City. Lothal is noted for its drainage. Rakhigarhi has been only partly excavated.

Mohenjo-daro and Harappa are in Pakistan, and finds such as the Dancing Girl were divided at Partition. India received the Dancing Girl, and Pakistan received the Priest-King. The pin for Mohenjo-daro is shown because it is the find-spot.

history.what: The Indus civilisation begins, per Wikipedia. Newer research suggests Dholavira was occupied as early as about 3500 BCE.
The mature phase of the cities.
Decline of the cities. Dholavira is reoccupied after a short break until about 1450 BCE, by the usual account.
The bronze Dancing Girl is found at Mohenjo-daro.
The Pashupati seal is found at Mohenjo-daro.
J. P. Joshi of the ASI officially discovers Dholavira.
ASI excavations begin at Dholavira under R. S. Bisht.
Dholavira is inscribed by UNESCO.

future: Training: ASI, universities and site museums train archaeologists and guides. Local people can be part of this.
Livelihood: the World Heritage listing of Dholavira brings visitors to a remote Kutch area. Fair local jobs and craft sales matter.
Materials: replicas in clay and bronze give craft workers a link to this heritage, if they are labelled as modern.
Documentation: the script is unread, so every new inscription and its find-spot should be published.
Protection: sites need drainage, fencing and watch against looting. The status of some finds between India and Pakistan is still raised in public debate.
